extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and documenting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, including what prior art may be relied upon, how to determine analogous art, how to compare claimed inventions to the prior art, and how to consider applicant replies and rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant reply requirements (37 CFR 1.111(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. If an applicant disagrees with factual findings, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred substantively. Mere statements that the Office has not established a prima facie case or unsupported assertions about common knowledge are not substantively adequate. Examiners may repeat the rejection and make the next action final if the traverse is ineffective. See MPEP §706.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant’s rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence that is timely presented by the applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others) and evidence of unexpected results. Applicants may also submit evidence that one of ordinary skill could not have combined claimed elements by known methods (technological difficulties), that elements in combination do not merely perform separate functions, or that results were unexpected. Once rebuttal evidence is presented, examiners should reconsider obviousness in view of the entire record, articulate findings of fact supporting conclusions, review all rejections and proposed rejections for continued viability, and follow procedures in MPEP §706.07(a). See MPEP §2145 and §§716–716.10 regarding affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under section 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is based on the type of prior art reference used and its applicable statutory category (e.g., 102(a)(1), (a)(2), pre-AIA 102(a), 102(b), 102(e), etc.). Admitted prior art may be relied upon for anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of whether it otherwise qualifies under statutory categories. For an overview of what constitutes prior art and related provisions see MPEP §§901–901.06(d), §§2121–2129, and §§2151–2155. In some cases, a publication applied under pre-AIA 102(a) may be overcome by a sworn statement under 37 CFR 1.131.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content of the prior art (enablement, inoperative devices, admissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive content of the prior art involves issues like availability of inoperative devices, the extent to which prior art must be enabling, whether broad disclosure suffices versus preferred embodiments, and admissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consult MPEP §§2121–2129 for case law and guidance on these topics and apply those principles when determining what the prior art teaches or discloses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine prior art content as of the time the invention was made (avoid hindsight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content of the prior art is determined at the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers must 'cast the mind back to the time the invention was made' and avoid using knowledge of the claimed invention to read back into the prior art. See cases such as W.L. Gore & Associates v. Garlock for the admonition against hindsight. See MPEP §2145 for discussion of rebutting hindsight-based applicant arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — evidence and burdens to avail benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to avail of benefits of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) bears the burden of establishing that subject matter used in a rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avail joint research provisions, applicant must establish (A) the invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement effective on or before the invention date, (B) the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of that agreement, and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the agreement. See MPEP §706.02(l)(1)-(2) and cases such as In re Bartfeld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art requirement for 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is analogous if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). 'Reasonably pertinent' means the reference would logically have commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering the problem. Examiner may consider the problem as reflected in the specification and may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support pertinence. If the problem is perceived too narrowly inconsistent with the specification, available prior art may be improperly limited; examiners should explain why an inventor seeking to solve the identified problem would have looked to the reference. See KSR, In re Bigio, In re ICON, In re Clay, and In re Klein.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner should consider similarities and differences in structure and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarities and differences in structure and function of inventions carry greater weight than classification cross-references in determining analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office classification and cross-references are some evidence, but courts place greater weight on structural/functional similarities (see In re Ellis). Examiners should analyze structural and functional overlap when deciding whether art is analogous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous-art analysis is technology-specific (chemical/mechanical/electrical/design examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy may be determined differently in various arts; examples illustrate how courts have treated analogous art in chemical, mechanical, electrical, and design arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For chemical arts, teachings concerning absorbing biologically active materials on carriers or dye chemistry may be pertinent; for mechanical arts, a broad spectrum of prior art is appropriate when similar problems exist; for electrical arts, solutions to rate-limiting problems in different high-frequency devices may be pertinent; for design arts, a prior design is of the type claimed if it has the same general use as that claimed. See cited cases (Ex parte Bland; Stratoflex; In re Mlot-Fijalkowski; Stevenson; Medtronic; In re Rosen; Ex parte Pappas; In re Butera). Use these precedents to inform analogous-art determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting claims and determining differences between prior art and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining differences between the prior art and the claims requires interpreting claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consult MPEP §§2111–2116.01 for claim interpretation law and MPEP §2143.03 for examples of claim language issues. The analysis must consider all claim limitations and the references as complete disclosures, not isolated features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claimed invention 'as a whole' in obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not focus solely on isolated differences; consider how the combination of features operates together and whether the 'as a whole' subject matter would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill. Cases such as Stratoflex, Schenck, and In re Hirao illustrate that admitted unobviousness of some claim parts can make the combination nonobvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill to a 'gist' or 'thrust' of an invention (avoid improper abstraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the statutory requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting consideration to a single feature or purported advantage and disregarding express claim limitations is improper (see W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb v. Barnes-Hind/Hydrocurve; Jones v. Hardy; Panduit). Examiners must apply the full scope of claim limitations in the obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of the source/cause of a problem is part of the 'as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of the source of a problem can itself be the patentable inventive contribution, even if the remedy would be obvious after that discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining whether discovery of a problem's cause renders the claimed invention patentable requires analyzing the invention as a whole. However, if the prior art already contains the same solution for a similar problem, discovery may not result in patentability. See In re Sponnoble and In re Wiseman for examples and limits of this principle.
